country.comment: Empirical analysis uses Brazilian Population Census (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000) and IBGE municipal survey (1999, 2005) data for Brazilian urban areas; China, Indonesia, and the United States are discussed only as comparative background.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Section 1; PDF p. 7, Section 2.1

effect_estimate.comment: All numeric estimates are extracted strictly from the readable manuscript text (note that end-of-paper Tables 1-8, A1, and B2 on PDF pp. 39-46, 48, and 50 are embedded graphics without extracted text, so unprinted cell SEs/CIs are not inferred).
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive coverage & disparities: Across urbanized Brazilian localities (>=50% urban), household central water connection coverage rose from 51% in 1970 to 89% in 2000 (51% to 92% in the constant sample of 258 localities), and full service (electricity, central water, and central sewer) rose from 25% to 49%; in 1980, only 61% of small (1-2 room) houses vs. 86% of large (6-7 room) houses had a central water connection (17% vs. 54% for full service), and in 1991 unweighted central water coverage was 57% for small (1-3 room) houses vs. 89% for large (7-9 room) houses, with households not owning the land under their homes worst served. Strategic municipal under-servicing (1991 small-house central water share, mean 0.77): With urban-area fixed effects and inverse-density weights, rival localities' water servicing has a strategic reaction slope of beta = -0.43 in lagged OLS and beta = -0.53 in spatial MLE (-0.69 OLS and -0.59 MLE with equal weights), meaning a 1 percentage point increase in rival localities' small-house water servicing reduces own-locality small-house water servicing by ~0.45 percentage points; moving from lowest to highest locality income and size quintiles raises servicing by 0.48 (48 percentage points) before interaction, but the top-income by 4th/5th-size quintile interaction reduces this gain by 0.16 (16 percentage points), and marginal income and scale effects become negative in large, rich localities in the 23-urban-area subsample (effects vanish in 1991 large-house and 2000 post-democratization small-house counterfactuals). Impact on 1991-2000 locality household growth (N = 351 MCAs in 55 urban areas, mean growth 0.40): Instrumenting 1991 small-house central water servicing with porous geology and insolation (first-stage partial F ~ 13) reverses biased negative OLS estimates to +0.74 in 2SLS (+0.77 with shorter instrument list; +0.78 with river/altitude instruments; p < 0.10) and ~+0.8 in LIML (significant at just over the 5% level), where a 1 SD (0.21) increase in small-house water servicing raises decade household growth by 0.17 (and a 1 SD reduction lowers 2SLS low-educated household growth by 0.17, with a similarly large positive IV effect on high-educated household growth at just over the 5% level). Using the share of untitled houses with central water yields weak instruments (partial F = 6.2; OLS -0.16, LIML 1.82, SE = 2.22, insignificant). Rent hedonics (1980): Central water connection commands a 12% rent premium in Sao Paulo and 23% in Rio de Janeiro; central sewer commands 9% and 18% premiums over no connection.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (Documented association): Although Section 5 uses IV (2SLS/LIML) to estimate how water coverage affects population growth, the study suffers from Serious risk of bias under ROBINS-I (exclusionary policy is proxied ecologically by the share of 1-3 room houses with central water regardless of legal/tenure status; first-stage joint IV strength is modest at partial F ~ 13 with 2SLS p < 0.10, and the untitled-housing specification has F = 6.2 and is insignificant), and the legal/administrative mechanisms affecting water access itself (pre-1988 illegality of servicing informal settlements, >125 sq m minimum lot-size zoning, tenure status, and strategic municipal withholding) are analyzed via indirect statistical/descriptive associations and lagged spatial regressions rather than direct empirical observation of municipal connection procedures or denials.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 6, Section 1; PDF pp. 12-14, Sections 2.4-2.5; PDF pp. 23-33, Sections 4-5

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines pre-1988 legal prohibitions on providing central water/sewer to untitled favelas and zoning-noncompliant loteamentos (tenure, property), national (125 sq m) and stricter local minimum lot-size zoning laws (zoning), neighborhood-targeted spatial under-provision of central water networks (service_area), strategic municipal discretion in withholding/expanding infrastructure and post-1988 regularization/upgrading reforms (discretion), and inter-municipal fiscal/service competition across fragmented metropolitan jurisdictions alongside conflicting local, state, and federal incentives (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Selected ROBINS-I because the core causal empirical analysis evaluates local public water-servicing policy as a non-randomized municipal policy intervention across multi-locality urban areas using instrumental variables (2SLS and LIML) with urban-area fixed effects, complemented by lagged-covariate/spatial MLE reaction functions and pre/post-democratization (1991 vs. 2000) and large-house counterfactuals.
risk_of_bias_tool.where_found: PDF pp. 20-28, Section 4; PDF pp. 28-35, Section 5

sample_size.comment: Also reports descriptive subsamples of 429 urbanized localities in 1990/1991 and a constant panel of 258 localities >=50% urbanized in 1970 (PDF p. 11), robustness checks dropping 25 multi-municipality MCAs where the dominant municipality has <65% of urban population (PDF pp. 8, 27, 33), and 1980 rental hedonic regressions across 56 districts in Sao Paulo and 24 districts in Rio de Janeiro (PDF p. 47; exact rental-unit N in Table A1 on PDF p. 48 is in an unextracted graphic).
sample_size.value: 447 localities (Minimum Comparable Areas, comprising 659 municipalities in 1991) across 123 urban areas (1970, 1980, 1991, and 2000 censuses); main regression sample: 351 localities (MCAs) in 55 urban areas; restricted strategic-interaction subsample: 23 urban areas (10 with 2 localities and 13 with 3 localities)
sample_size.where_found: PDF pp. 7-8, Section 2.1 and Footnote 6; PDF p. 11, Section 2.4; PDF p. 26, Section 4.1.2; PDF p. 35, Section 6

study_design.comment: Combines a formal spatial-equilibrium fiscal competition model (Section 3) with multi-decade locality panel/cross-sectional econometric analyses of strategic water-servicing determinants (Section 4), IV estimates of servicing impacts on locality population growth and educational composition (Section 5), and hedonic rent regressions (Appendix A).
study_design.value: Quasi-experimental and spatial econometric multi-decade locality study using Brazilian Population Census data (1970, 1980, 1991, 2000) and municipal surveys (1999, 2005): (1) OLS with lagged covariates and spatial maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) with urban-area fixed effects for municipal strategic water-servicing reaction functions; (2) instrumental variables (2SLS and LIML) regressions with urban-area fixed effects estimating the effect of 1991 small-house water servicing on 1991-2000 locality household growth; and (3) 1980 cross-sectional hedonic rent regressions with district fixed effects
study_design.where_found: PDF pp. 7-8, Section 2.1; PDF pp. 20-24, Section 4; PDF pp. 28-32, Section 5; PDF p. 47, Appendix A
